blogs.title: How to Get a 5% Fixed Mortgage Rate in a 7% Market
blogs.excerpt: Right now the housing market is in a standoff. Rates are parked in the 7s, buyers are waiting for a deal, and sellers are refusing to slash their price. Homes sit. Everyone waits. If you have shopped for a home this year, you have felt it.
blogs.content:
Right now the housing market is in a standoff. Rates are parked in the 7s, buyers are waiting for a deal, and sellers are refusing to slash their price. Homes sit. Everyone waits. If you have shopped for a home this year, you have felt it. So when you finally find a home you like, the standard move is to negotiate the price down. Get the seller to knock off 5 or 6 percent and call it a win. It feels like the obvious play. Here is the problem: a price cut is one of the weakest ways to spend a seller’s money. There is a move that costs the seller the exact same dollars and puts far more of them in your pocket, every single month, for as long as you own the home.

You Are Negotiating for the Wrong Thing

When you push a seller for a lower price, you are chipping at the wrong number. A price reduction shrinks your loan a little. But your interest rate, the number that actually drives your monthly payment, does not move at all. There is a second option most buyers never bring up: ask the seller for a concession and aim those same dollars at your interest rate instead of the sticker price. We call this a seller-paid payment subsidy. You use the seller’s money to buy your rate down for the life of the loan. Same seller. Same dollars leaving their side of the table. Wildly different outcome for you.

Seller-Paid Payment Subsidy: Get a 5% Fixed Mortgage Rate in a 7% Market

Say you are buying a $500,000 home with 10% down. You have negotiated hard, and the seller is willing to give up 6%, which is $30,000. That $30,000 can go one of two ways. Option one: take it as a price cut. Option two: take it as a concession and use it to permanently buy down your rate. Watch what happens.
Market Rate Full price 6% Price Reduction 6% Concession 30-Yr Fixed 6% Concession 5-Yr ARM
Purchase Price $500,000 $470,000 $500,000 $500,000
Down Payment $50,000 $47,000 $50,000 $50,000
Loan Amount $450,000 $423,000 $450,000 $450,000
Interest Rate 6.750% 6.750% 5.375% 4.490%
APR* *7.050% *7.054% *5.670% *4.782%
Monthly Payment** $3,299.93 $3,101.93 $2,900.98 $2,658.42
Cash to Close $57,190 $54,190 $57,190 $57,190
Monthly Savings $0 $198.00 $398.95 $641.51
Savings (60 months) $0 $9,169 $31,034 $50,842

*APR is illustrative. **Payment includes estimated mortgage insurance. All figures are illustrative examples for a $500,000 purchase with 10% down; your actual numbers will vary with credit, program, and current pricing.

  Read that table again slowly, because the gap is bigger than most people expect.
  • Full price, market rate (baseline): 750% rate, about $3,299.93 a month.
  • 6% price reduction: the price drops to $470,000, but your rate stays at 6.750%. Payment falls to $3,101.93, a savings of $198 a month.
  • 6% concession, 30-year fixed: the price stays at $500,000, and the $30,000 buys your rate down to 5.375%. Payment drops to $2,900.98, a savings of $398.95 a month.
  • 6% concession, 5-year ARM: the same $30,000, aimed at an adjustable structure, buys the rate down to 4.490%. Payment of $2,658.42, a savings of $641.51 a month.
Same $30,000 from the seller. The price cut saves you $198 a month. The concession, on a fixed rate, saves you twice that. We will come back to the ARM in a minute, but the headline is simple: taking the money as a rate buydown beats taking it off the price, and it is not close.

Why the Lower Rate Wins by So Much

When you knock 6% off the price, most of that cut does not even touch your loan. You were only financing 90% of the price to begin with, so a lower price also means a smaller down payment. The actual reduction to your loan balance is about $27,000, and at 6.75% that trims your payment by only around $198. You save interest on that one small slice of principal, and that is it. When you take the 6% as a seller concession and buy down the rate, those dollars go to work on the entire loan. A lower rate applies to all $450,000 you borrowed, not a $27,000 sliver, and it keeps working every month for as long as you keep the loan. That is why the same money produces two, three, even four times the monthly savings. You are not shaving a corner off the balance. You are lowering the price of the money itself. One important distinction: this is a permanent buydown, not a temporary teaser. A temporary buydown (you may have heard of a “2-1 buydown”) lowers your rate for the first year or two and then springs back up. A permanent buydown locks the lower rate in for the full term. The 5.375% in that example is the rate in year one and in year twenty. *A quick note on the rules: seller concessions are capped by loan guidelines based on your down payment. On a primary residence with 10% down, the typical ceiling is 6% of the price. That is why this example uses 6%. You are putting the maximum allowable contribution to work in the smartest possible place.

The Five-Year and Fifteen-Year Picture

The monthly number is only the start. Stretch it out and the gap compounds.   Over the first five years, the price cut saves about $9,169. The concession on a fixed rate saves $31,034. That is real money you keep instead of handing to the bank in interest. Look fifteen years out at total interest and mortgage insurance paid, and the market-rate loan costs about $419,601, while the fixed-rate buydown drops that to $328,536. You are talking roughly $90,000 in lifetime interest, redirected from the lender back to you, all funded by a concession you were going to negotiate for anyway. This is the same principle behind why sitting on the sidelines rarely pays. If you have been holding out for the market to hand you a 5% rate, waiting is itself a bet, and this is how you build that rate yourself, today.

What About That 5-Year ARM?

You saw it in the comparison: the same 6& subsidy aimed at a 5-year ARM buys the rate all the way down to 4.490% and saves $641.51 a month. That is the biggest number on the page. For the right buyer, it can be a smart play. If you know you are likely to sell or refinance inside five years, or you are an entrepreneur who wants to keep maximum cash flow free for your business in the near term, the ARM squeezes more out of every concession dollar. But we lead with the fixed rate for a reason. An ARM adjusts after the initial five years, and where it lands depends on the market at that time. The 30-year fixed buydown gives you most of the benefit with none of the reset risk. Certainty has value. Whether the ARM fits comes down to your timeline and your appetite for risk, and that is a conversation to have with an advisor, not a decision to make off a chart.

The Step This Whole Strategy Depends On

Here is the part nobody puts on the comparison chart: none of this matters if you cannot get approved in the first place. And that is exactly where entrepreneurs get stuck. You built a profitable business, you take smart deductions, you reinvest, and then a traditional lender looks at your tax return, sees a shrunk-down taxable income, and tells you “no.” The concession strategy is useless if the same old lending model disqualifies you before you ever get to structure the deal. You are not hard to finance. You are just talking to the wrong lender. At NEO, we qualify entrepreneurs on their real financial picture, not the minimized version your CPA worked hard to build for tax season. Bank statement loans, 1099 programs, asset-based qualification, and DSCR loans let us approve you on actual cash flow. (Here is how entrepreneur mortgage programs evaluate cash flow instead of tax returns.) Put the two together and you have the whole play: an approval built for how entrepreneurs actually earn, plus a concession strategy that hands you a rate in the 5s in a 7% market. That is not waiting for the market to improve. That is engineering your own better deal.

The Bottom Line

Every home and every seller is different, and so is every buyer’s tax picture, timeline, and cash position. The numbers above are illustrative, but the strategy is real, and it works far more often than buyers realize. You have worked too hard to leave that kind of money on the table by negotiating for the wrong thing.

Seller-Paid Payment Subsidy FAQ

Is a seller concession the same as a price reduction? ▼
No. A price reduction lowers the sticker price of the home, which shrinks your loan a little but leaves your interest rate untouched. A concession is money the seller agrees to contribute toward your side of the deal. When you point that concession at a permanent rate buydown, it lowers your rate for the life of the loan, which works on the entire balance instead of a small slice of principal.
What is a permanent buydown, and how is it different from a 2-1 buydown? ▼
A permanent buydown uses points to lower your note rate for the full loan term. A 2-1 buydown is temporary: it drops your rate for the first year or two and then it climbs back to the original rate. The example in this article is a permanent buydown, so the lower rate is the same in year one and in year twenty.
How much can a seller contribute toward my costs? ▼
It depends on your loan type and how much you put down. On a primary residence with 10% down, the cap is commonly 6% of the price, which is why this example uses 6%. Put more down and the allowable contribution can rise. We will confirm the exact limit for your program and structure so you use every allowable dollar.
Should I choose the 5-year ARM or the 30-year fixed? ▼
The ARM buys the rate down furthest and saves the most in the near term, but it adjusts after five years, so its later cost depends on the market at that time. The 30-year fixed gives you most of the benefit with none of the reset risk. If you expect to sell or refinance within five years the ARM can make sense; if you value certainty, the fixed is the safer anchor. It comes down to your timeline and your comfort with risk.
I am self-employed and my tax returns show low income. Can I still use this? ▼
Yes. The concession strategy sits on top of your loan approval, and approval is exactly where entrepreneurs get stuck when a lender reads only a minimized tax return. At NEO we qualify you on your real financial picture using bank statement loans, 1099 programs, asset-based qualification, and DSCR loans, then structure the concession on top. You are not hard to finance. You are just talking to the wrong lender.
